items.title: Piaget underestimated young children's abilities
items.claim: Piaget's three-mountains task (1956) found children under 7 are 'egocentric' — unable to take another's perspective. What did later work show?

options.text: Piaget's stages are timed exactly correctly

When the task is made more naturalistic (Hughes's policeman doll task, 1975), 3-4 year olds succeed; Piaget's task underestimated perspective-taking ability. False-belief tasks (Wimmer & Perner 1983) reveal more nuanced developmental trajectories

items.reveal:
Martin Hughes's 1975 'naughty boy hiding from policeman' task gave familiar context: ~90% of 3-4 year olds succeeded. Theory of mind (false belief) emerges around age 4; precursors are present earlier in non-verbal tasks (Onishi & Baillargeon 2005).

Piaget's broader staircase model — distinct, age-defined stages with sharp transitions — has been replaced by more gradualist accounts in modern developmental cognitive neuroscience.
items.why: Famous developmental milestones can shift dramatically with task design. Children often know more than the original tasks could reveal.

items.title: The bystander effect story
items.claim: Darley and Latane (1968) showed that people are less likely to help when others are present. The often-repeated 'Kitty Genovese 38 witnesses' story has been challenged. What did later journalism find?
items.prompt: Which is closest to the current historical record?

options.text: There were probably far fewer witnesses than reported, and some did call police
There were no witnesses at all

items.reveal:
Manning, Levine and Collins (2007) and later reporting by the New York Times showed the original 1964 article overstated the number of witnesses and inattention.

The bystander effect as a laboratory phenomenon is robust, but the case used to illustrate it was inaccurate.
items.why: Findings can be real while their iconic illustrations are not. Textbooks now distinguish the experimental effect from the journalistic story.

items.title: The lobotomy was awarded a Nobel Prize
items.claim: Egas Moniz won the 1949 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his discovery of the therapeutic value of the prefrontal leucotomy (lobotomy). What's the modern status?

options.text: The procedure remains a first-line treatment

Lobotomy is no longer performed; thousands of patients (around 40,000-50,000 in the US alone, 1936-50s) suffered permanent personality damage. Modern psychosurgery is far more targeted (deep brain stimulation, cingulotomy for refractory OCD)

items.reveal_title: An honoured procedure that caused immense harm
items.reveal:
Walter Freeman performed perhaps 3,500 of his transorbital 'icepick' lobotomies in the US through the 1950s. Patients included Rosemary Kennedy (1941, permanently incapacitated) and many institutionalised individuals.

The procedure declined rapidly after chlorpromazine (1952) provided pharmacological alternatives. Calls to revoke Moniz's Nobel continue. Modern functional neurosurgery (capsulotomy, cingulotomy, deep brain stimulation) targets specific circuits with imaging guidance and is reversible (in DBS).
items.why: Therapeutic enthusiasm without rigorous evidence can produce widespread harm. Modern evidence-based standards exist because of cases like this.
